newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: AFRICAN BUSINESS ON AGENDA AT ZIMBABWE SUMMIT.
newsitem.headline: AFRICAN BUSINESS ON AGENDA AT ZIMBABWE SUMMIT.

text.p: African leaders meet top United States businessmen in Zimbabwe this week to discuss business opportunities in the world's poorest continent.

U.S. President Bill Clinton is sending a delegation led by civil rights leader Jesse Jackson and Transportation Secretary Rodney Slater to the four-day summit of African leaders and black Americans, opening in Harare on Tuesday.

Conference organisers hope the Fourth African/African- American Summit will help boost investment in Africa by facilitating personal contact between dozens of U.S. chief executive officers and African presidents and captains of industry.

Host Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe, Laurent Kabila of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire), Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and Organisation of African Unity (OAU) Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim are among the over 30 African leaders expected at the meeting.

Besides Jackson and Slater, the American delegation includes the chief exeutives of Fortune 500 companies such as Owens-Corning , Chrysler Corporation , Colgate-Palmolive , Kellogg Company , Chevron Corporation , and Procter and Gamble Company .

The conference is convened by Leon Sullivan, an American civil rights activist who has over the last two decades championed a campaign to promote U.S.-African relations and who believes it is in the interest of Americans to increase investment in Africa.

"hose who have and can, have an obligation to uplift those who don't have. Poverty breeds instability locally and globally and it makes business sense to undercut that through increased investment and promoting sustainable economic growth,'' Sullivan said during a trip to Zimbabwe early this year.

U.S. ambassador to Zimbabwe Johnnie Carson told reporters Washington shared this view, saying: "The continuing message and focus of Washington in Africa shows through different, but strong lines. There remains a high-core constituency in America that is interested in Africa. It is more stronger, broader and diverse.''
The summit will run workshps that will look at various sectors, including health, agriculture, manufacturing, information, mining and education.
Africa remains the poorest continent despite efforts by some of its leaders in the past decade to improve the situation.

The continent's average real growth rate has increased from less than one percent in 1992 to over 5.5 percent in 1996. But the rise has largely been in the primary products sector -- particularly agriculture -- reflecting good rains in several countries and an upswing in commodity prices.

The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) say investor interest in Africa is slowly rising, but the figures are still low. For example, foreign direct investment into southern Africa averaged just $90 million per country in 1995 compared to nearly $4.5 billion for Hungary.

Many economic analysts believe African states can only sustain investor interest through political stability and economic reforms such as privatisation, exchange control liberalisation and curbing government spending.
